job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior tax associate at McAllister and Co, a small accountancy practice in Glasgow with eleven people. I prepare personal and small business tax returns and check every figure against the client's papers. I rent a room in a flat in Partick with two other women and take the train in. I like finishing a return and knowing it's right, and I like a quiet desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we'll see, maybe some software upgrades. To friends I'd say I've heard this before, with cloud accounting and tablets. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm half relieved. Our tax software already pre-fills boxes and I double-check every one by hand, because the one time it got a figure wrong I caught it. I'd rather it didn't touch my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my tax exams and put in the hours. I'd save three hundred and fifty a month and keep my room in the flat share. And I'd keep doing returns the careful way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about losing the job, just that the routine returns I do are the easiest part to hand to software, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check everything by hand. Does that slow you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. Rhona (my senior) says I'm thorough but slower than Callum, who uses the shortcuts. I'd rather be right and slow. If a client gets a penalty because of my speed, it's my name on the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries would remain even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the firm is small, and one big client leaving would hurt. And Glasgow rents rise every year. My dad says I should think about buying in five years, but I can't see it yet.

say: I'd tell colleagues we'll see; maybe some **software upgrades**, nothing more.
I'd tell friends I've heard this before, with cloud accounting and tablets.
think: I'm half **relieved**, since I check every box by hand and trust my own work.
The routine returns I prepare are still the easiest thing to hand to software.
do: Carry on with the **tax exams** and keep preparing returns the careful way.
Save **£350 a month** and keep my room in the flat share.
feel: **Uneasy**; not about the job itself but about how routine my daily work is.
S0.quote: I'd rather be right and slow. If a client gets a penalty because of my speed, it's my name on the file.
fieldNote: Prizes **being right** over speed, which her senior reads as slow.
Small firm of eleven means **one lost client** would hurt, with or without AI.
Rising **rent** keeps buying a flat out of sight.

steps.text: Keep sitting the tax exams on schedule
Keep checking every return by hand before it goes out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's look at which tasks move and keep careful checks on the output. To friends I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not. Online I'd say nothing, I don't enjoy debates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I know returns and data entry go first. Rhona told us the firm is trialling a tool for client data. I'd be the one checking its output all day, and I don't know if that job is worth a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tool, grudgingly, since I can't check what I don't understand. I'd push on with my tax exams, because advice work is harder to automate. And I'd ask Rhona to put me in client meetings, so I'm not hidden behind a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My pay is fine now, but the entry level of this job is exactly what they'd shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it grudgingly. What's the grudge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pushed into it. I like knowing how a number got where it is. A tool that gives me an answer and no workings goes against what I was taught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the firm hires fewer juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure I'd blame anyone. The partners have a business to run and the software firms sell what they sell. But the professional bodies should say what training juniors must still get, or there won't be any seniors later.

say: I'd say let's work out which tasks move and **check the output** carefully.
I'd tell friends it's coming whether we like it or not, and avoid debates.
think: Returns and data entry go first, so my daily work is **exposed**.
Checking a tool's output all day may not be a job worth a salary.
do: Learn the firm's **data tool**, grudgingly, since I can't check what I don't understand.
Push on with the tax exams towards **advice work**.
Ask Rhona for more client meetings.
feel: **Anxious**; pay is fine now but entry-level tasks are exactly what firms shrink.
S1.quote: The professional bodies should say what training juniors must still get, or there won't be any seniors later.
fieldNote: Learns the tool out of need, not curiosity, and resents **answers without workings**.
Looks for blame and finds **no single culprit**, then points to the professional bodies.
Moves towards **people-facing** work to stay out of reach of software.

steps.text: Learn the firm's client data tool well enough to check it
Push on with the tax exams towards advice work
Ask Rhona to put me in client meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk about what the firm does in two years. To friends I'd say I don't know what to say, which is true. Online nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I picked a profession that gets cleared out first. Two years is not enough to switch, and I've spent four on this. I don't use these tools, so I'd be behind on top of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs at once: move to a cheaper room, no holidays, save eight hundred a month. I'd start using the AI tools every day, because refusing helps no one. And I'd ask my dad whether his pharmacy needs a bookkeeper, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be short of sleep and snappy. I'm a planner, and this leaves no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away the exam years that pay off later. A tax qualification takes three more years for me. By then the thing it qualifies me for might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, who runs a nursery, that I'd be fine for a year, and mean it for about six months. I'd tell my dad the truth. He'd say come home, and I'd probably take him up on it.

say: I'd say the firm needs to **talk now** about what it does in two years.
I'd tell friends I honestly don't know what to say.
think: I picked the profession that gets **cleared out first**, and two years is too short to switch.
I don't use the tools, so I'm behind on top of everything.
do: Move to a **cheaper room**, drop holidays and save **£800** a month.
Start using AI tools **every day**, because refusing helps no one.
Ask my dad if his pharmacy needs a bookkeeper.
feel: **Alarmed**; short of sleep and snappy, because I'm a planner with no plan.
S2.quote: I'm a planner, and this leaves no plan.
fieldNote: Her **habit of waiting** for proof meets a clock she cannot wait out.
Expects the tax qualification to be worthless by the time she finishes.
Would likely **go home** to her father, though she says it with reluctance.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper room in a smaller flat share
Use the AI tools every day at work
Ask my dad about bookkeeping work at his pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years lets us retrain people properly, if the firm plans. To friends I'd say I'm keeping an eye on it. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the job as I know it is gone by the end. The question is whether I find the next one before it goes. I'd rather look early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning the tools in the first year and take client-facing tasks. I'd finish the tax exams, then think about moving into tax advice for families. And I'd keep saving, aiming for a year's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a handle on it. Five years gives me a year or two to adjust and a few to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is that different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm reacting. With five, I can be deliberate, though I'm not naturally quick at it. I'd still lose the first year doing nothing, probably, which is the habit I'd have to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you lose a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I tend to wait until something is proven. I watched my friends pick up tools two years ago and thought I'd wait. Waiting felt sensible, and it turns out I'm behind.

say: I'd say five years lets us **retrain people** properly, if the firm plans.
I'd tell friends I'm keeping an eye on it and say little online.
think: The job as I know it is gone by the end, so I must find the **next one** early.
My habit of waiting for proof is my biggest risk.
do: Start learning the tools in year one and take **client-facing tasks**.
Finish the tax exams, then move into **tax advice** for families.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a handle on it, since five years allows a plan.
S3.quote: With two years, I'm reacting. With five, I can be deliberate, though I'm not naturally quick at it.
fieldNote: Knows her **slowness** is the weak point and names it unprompted.
Plans a move into **advice work** where she talks to clients.
Longer timeline turns alarm into worry she can act on.

steps.text: Start learning the firm's AI tools in the first year
Finish the tax exams and take client-facing tasks
Move towards tax advice work for families
Save up a year of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is long, so no panic. To friends I'd say I'll deal with it when it gets closer. Online nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly safe for a while, but still a little uneasy. I'd be thirty-two. I might have a family and a mortgage by then, and a job that has changed beyond recognition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams, then move into advice work that needs me to talk to people. I'd learn the tools bit by bit. I'd save for a flat and start a pension early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. Ten years is far enough that I'd stop checking the news about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your future employer to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell staff early and pay for retraining. I wouldn't ask for much. Just warning and a fair chance to learn, since I'm slow to pick things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting accounting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the exams still matter, and to learn the people side, because the number side will be done by machines. And not to copy my habit of waiting.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so **no panic**.
I'd tell friends I'll deal with it when it gets closer.
think: I'd feel **mostly safe** for a while, but a little uneasy about a job changed beyond recognition.
By thirty-two I might have a family and a mortgage.
do: Finish the exams, then move into **advice work** that needs talking to people.
Save for a flat and start a **pension** early.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, because ten years is far enough off.
S4.quote: Ten years is far enough that I'd stop checking the news about it.
fieldNote: Slow to act, so ten years suits her; she is **steady** rather than relieved.
Asks only for **early warning** and a fair chance to learn.
Her advice to a cousin is the opposite of her **own habit**.

steps.text: Finish the tax exams and move into advice work
Learn the AI tools one task at a time
Save for a flat and start a pension early
Keep studying for the next professional qualification

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years leaves no plan, and I'm the person who needs one. Warning from firms and paid retraining would help, and the professional bodies keeping junior training in place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I know I'm slow to change and I'm working on it. I'd rather be careful than quick, but careful can't turn into late.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be careful than quick, but careful can't turn into late.
portrait: Priya is a **22-year-old tax associate** in Glasgow, top of her class, with no debt and a family net.
She never uses AI tools and **checks everything** by hand, which her colleagues call slow.
She blames **nobody in particular** and looks to the professional bodies to keep junior training.
Her mood runs from **uneasy to alarmed** as the warning shrinks, and eases at ten years.
She knows her **habit of waiting** is her risk and is trying to fight it.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because she is a planner and two years leaves no plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** from firms and paid retraining.
The **professional bodies** keeping junior training in place.
